title: Digging for Answers
theme: Research and inquiry: finding and checking sources
objectives: I can describe each step of a research project with a precise word.
I can decide whether a source is reputable and whether a fact is relevant.
I can explain how to verify a claim and cite where it came from.
I can write a short plan for an inquiry using at least five words from this unit.
rationale: Sustained research writing is new in grade 7, and students need words for each stage. Asking (inquiry), gathering (survey, compile, consult), judging (verify, authentic, reputable, relevant), and crediting (source, cite) form one routine students can say aloud and reuse across subjects. Two words carry a second meaning students will meet elsewhere: source also names where a river begins, and survey can be a verb meaning to look over an area. The unit reaches back to the tone words from unit 1, because a skeptical or cynical voice and an earnest one treat the same evidence differently.

passage.title: A Question About Hollis Creek
paras: Maya's inquiry began with a question she could not stop asking: why were there fewer minnows in Hollis Creek this year? Mr. Okoye, her science teacher, said a strong inquiry starts with a question that evidence can answer. She wrote it on an index card and taped it above her desk.

Her first job was to compile information. She borrowed old fishing logs from the library, ran a survey of twenty neighbors about when they had last seen minnows, and read the state wildlife agency's yearly counts. Soon she had more facts than she could use, and Mr. Okoye taught her to ask whether each one was relevant. A chart of last winter's snowfall in another state, for example, said nothing about her creek, so she set it aside.

The harder job was deciding what to trust. One website claimed that a nearby farm had poisoned the water, but it listed no author, no date, and no sources, and Maya doubted that it was reputable. A photograph on the page showed dead fish under a bridge, yet she could not tell whether the picture was authentic or had been taken somewhere else. She tried to verify the claim by comparing it with the agency's reports, which named their data, and those reports said nothing about poison.

Next she decided to consult an expert. Dr. Pham, a biologist at the county college, met with her and explained that a dry summer can shrink a creek's shallow pools and warm the water that is left. Small fish may then have too little cool water to survive. Maya wrote down the explanation and asked what evidence would support it.

In her final report, Maya cited every source in a list at the back, including her neighbors' survey, so that any reader could check her work. Her conclusion was careful: the dry summer was the most likely cause, but more counts next year would help. Mr. Okoye wrote a single line at the bottom: “Good inquiry ends with evidence, not certainty.”

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word “relevant” most nearly means
choices: recent and up to date
closely connected to the topic
surprising and unusual
easy to find in a library
qs.why: Maya sets aside the snowfall chart because it says nothing about her creek, so relevant means connected to her topic.

qs.q: Why did Maya doubt the website's claim about the farm?
choices: It was too long to read in one sitting.
It named too many experts she had never met.
It listed no author, no date, and no sources.
It was about a creek in a different state.
qs.why: The passage says the page gave no author, date, or sources, which are the signs of a source that cannot be checked.

qs.q: Which action best shows Maya trying to verify the website's claim?
choices: She compared the claim with the agency's reports.
She taped her question above her desk.
She ran a survey of twenty neighbors.
She asked Mr. Okoye to choose a new topic.
qs.why: Verifying means checking against a trusted source, and Maya compares the claim with reports that named their data.

qs.q: What does Dr. Pham's explanation suggest about the minnows?
choices: The farm poisoned the creek last winter.
Minnows prefer shallow, warm water.
The neighbors' survey must have been wrong.
A dry summer may have left them too little cool water.
qs.why: Dr. Pham says a dry summer can shrink pools and warm the water, so small fish may lack cool water.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: Good research gathers facts, tests them, and gives credit while staying honest about what is known.
Neighbors know more about creeks than scientists do.
Creeks change every year for the same reasons.
A photograph is always the best kind of evidence.
qs.why: Maya compiles, judges, consults, cites, and writes a careful conclusion; the passage is about that whole routine.

constructed.prompt: A friend sends you a surprising statistic and says, “I saw it online.” Explain how you would decide whether to trust it. Use source, verify, and reputable.

describes a second check against a trusted source
constructed.model: I would first ask for the original source of the statistic, not just where my friend saw it. Then I would verify the number by checking a reputable site, such as a government agency that explains how it collects data.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words that name the stages of a research project, read a short narrative about a student investigating a creek, and write a plan for an inquiry that includes checking and crediting sources. The words fit together as one routine: ask, gather, judge, credit.

notes.va.source.n: Distinguish source (where information comes from) from resource. Introduce the river sense briefly with a picture, since students meet it in geography. Have students rank three mystery sources, such as a diary, a rumor, and an encyclopedia, from least to most trustworthy.
notes.va.authentic.adj: Authentic means genuine, not merely good or traditional. Pair with a counterfeit or edited-image example. A likely mix-up is believing that anything authentic is also accurate; a real letter can still contain a mistake.
notes.va.verify.v: Verify is an action, not a feeling of being sure. Model a two-source check aloud. Ask students to name what they would do if the second source disagreed with the first.
notes.va.inquiry.n: An inquiry starts with a question that can be investigated. Have students revise vague questions (Why is the creek bad?) into answerable ones (Did the number of minnows change after 2020?). The family word inquire is a good link to everyday asking.
notes.va.survey.n: Teach both senses: the noun (asking many people) and the verb (looking over carefully). Discuss why a survey of twenty friends may not represent a whole school; this is revisited in unit 9.
notes.va.compile.v: Compile means gather from several places and combine. Ask what is lost if students only copy one source. Connect to a bibliography or a playlist as familiar examples.
notes.va.relevant.adj: Relevant is relative to a point. A fact is relevant to one claim and irrelevant to another. Give students five facts and two claims and have them match.
notes.va.consult.v: Consult is about asking for expertise or checking a trusted reference. Students may use it as a general synonym for talk to; keep the sense of advice or facts from someone or something that knows.
notes.va.reputable.adj: Reputable describes a source with a record of honesty and accuracy. Reputation alone is not proof: encourage students to verify even reputable sources when a claim is surprising.
notes.va.cite.v: Cite is often confused with the homophones site and sight. Use a three-word sentence set. Emphasize that citing gives credit and lets the reader check, not just a format rule.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “My question is whether the website is telling the truth. It has no author and no date, so I cannot tell where the information came from. I will verify the claim by comparing it with a reputable source that names its data. If the two disagree, I will consult an expert before I decide.”
discuss: Which step of a research project is hardest for you: asking, gathering, judging, or crediting? Why?
If a source is authentic but not relevant, should you still use it? Explain.
misconceptions: A source is always a website.
A reputable source is never wrong.
Citing is only for direct quotations.
extend: Compile a one-page source list on a topic from another class, marking each source as primary or secondary and as more or less reputable, with one sentence of reasoning.
Design a five-question survey on a school issue and predict one way the results might be misleading.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Link back to tone: ask whether a cynical, earnest, or sarcastic author changes how much to trust a source, and why tone is not the same as accuracy. Return to verify, reputable, and cite two days later in a short source-evaluation task, again at one week, and in unit 3 when students compile examples of number prefixes.

The fact about ___ is relevant to my topic because ___.
wida.oral: Partner A states a surprising claim. Partner B asks how they could verify it and what source they would consult, then restates the plan using two words from the unit.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: indagación (inquiry), pertinente (relevant; relevante is also standard), de buena reputación (reputable), recopilar (compile), fuente (source, the river sense also uses fuente or nacimiento).
Pronunciation of inquiry: the stress pattern IN-kwur-ee is also standard; this unit shows in-KWY-ur-ee.
Passage is fiction (invented creek and characters). The general statement that dry summers can shrink pools and warm water is true in broad terms but should be confirmed by a science reviewer.
